title: Pass Data Down and Send Events Up
summary: Split a small interface into a parent and child with clear ownership of state.
prerequisites: Complete the earlier Junior lessons and use only your personal learning org.
learningObjectives: Pass read-only data through public properties.
Communicate intent through a narrow event.

sections.heading: Give each component a responsibility
body: A component can become difficult to understand when it owns a list, renders every row, edits a record, and coordinates unrelated behaviour. Splitting it helps only when the responsibilities become clearer. For this exercise, appointmentPicker owns a small simulated list and the selected identifier. appointmentChoice displays one item and announces that the user selected it.

A public @api property lets the parent supply data to the child. The child should treat an object supplied by its owner as read-only. If it wants a change, it should communicate an intent rather than secretly altering the parent's object. This makes the direction of state ownership visible and makes later bugs easier to trace.

callouts.text: The owner decides the state. A child displays the supplied value and announces an action.

sections.heading: Use a small event contract
body: A CustomEvent communicates something that happened. Its type is a string agreed between sender and listener. In this example the type is selectappointment, and the detail is just the selected identifier. Sending a primitive identifier avoids exposing a mutable object when the parent only needs to know which item was chosen.

The child dispatches the event from itself. The parent listens directly on the child element with onselectappointment. The default non-bubbling, non-composed behaviour is sufficient for this direct relationship. Do not set every event to bubble across boundaries merely because it seems easier; a broader event contract exposes behaviour to more consumers.

The examples still use simulated rows so that you can understand communication independently of record access. The parent displays the chosen demonstration ID. It does not pass that ID into the real record form from J24. To integrate with actual data later, the parent must receive real accessible Salesforce IDs through an appropriate data path.

callouts.text: An event is a UI message, not proof of authorization or a database save.

sections.heading: Inspect the boundary rather than adding global variables
body: Create both component bundles. Give the child an API 68.0 metadata file with isExposed false, because it is used inside the parent. Expose the parent on a Lightning App Page using the configuration pattern from J23. Both bundles must be deployed, because the parent references the child by its kebab-case tag name.

Select the first row and then the second. The parent should display the corresponding ID each time. Inspect the child and confirm it does not assign to choice.id or change the supplied object. The parent remains the source of the selected state. A shared global variable is unnecessary for this local relationship.

Now deliberately mismatch the event name in a disposable local change. Observe that the child button can still respond internally while the parent never receives the agreed message. Restore the matching name. This is a useful debugging exercise because the visible symptom does not automatically imply a server problem.

If the interface grows beyond a direct parent-child relationship, other communication mechanisms may become appropriate. They belong to a different design discussion. For this small example, keep the contract narrow enough that you can explain every value crossing the component boundary.

callouts.text: Trace the selected ID from child event detail to parent state without mutating the incoming row object.

steps.instruction: Add the child and parent files with matching names and the appropriate exposure metadata.
steps.expected: The parent can render the child.

steps.instruction: Use both child buttons and observe the parent status text.
steps.expected: Each event carries the expected primitive ID.

steps.title: Inspect ownership
steps.instruction: Review assignments in both classes and perform the deliberate event-name mismatch test.
steps.expected: State ownership and the communication failure are explainable.

exercise.title: Build a two-component picker
exercise.brief: Extend the example with a third simulated item and document the public contract.
steps: Describe the child input and event detail.
Show that selecting each item updates only the parent-owned selection.
Record the mismatch symptom and its correction.
acceptance: The child does not mutate the supplied object.
Events use a clear matching name and minimal detail.
The simulation is not described as a database operation.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why send only the identifier?
knowledgeCheck.answer: It is the smallest information the parent needs and avoids exposing unnecessary mutable data.

knowledgeCheck.question: Do these direct events need global propagation?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. The parent listens directly to its child; wider propagation is unnecessary.
